evidence_cards.unit: hours per year per adult (mean over adults with a valid answer), or percent of adults
evidence_cards.definition: Edited annual hours adults report spending on their own visits and prescriptions, on others' visits, on medical bills and insurance, and on health care paperwork; plus the share who cared for a friend or family member in the past 30 days. evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.

MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire paper (N3C/RECOVER retrospective cohort study) characterizes use of ICD-10-CM code U09.9 ('Post COVID-19 condition, unspecified') and associated diagnoses, procedures, medications, and demographics; Lyme disease is never mentioned in the document body.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed study using the National COVID Cohort Collaborative (N3C) electronic health record database to examine how the new U09.9 long COVID diagnosis code was used by 34 US health systems between October 2021 and May 2022, in a base cohort of 33,782 patients. It reports who received the code (skewed toward female, White, non-Hispanic patients and those in lower-poverty, lower-unemployment areas), what conditions and procedures co-occurred with the diagnosis, and discusses how the nearly two-year delay before the code existed, inconsistent coding practice, and unequal access to the primary-care visits that generate the code likely mean the coded population undercounts and misrepresents the true long COVID population. It does not report any direct medical cost, non-medical cost, income loss, or caregiving-time figures.

contextual_issues: The paper notes it cannot distinguish clinical (problem-list) diagnosis codes from billing/reimbursement codes, meaning some U09.9 use may reflect administrative rather than clinical care-seeking burden, but this is not quantified.

Receipt of rehabilitation services (physical/occupational therapy) in the 60 days after U09.9 diagnosis is described as 'rising with patient age,' which the authors say 'lends insight into the burden of functional disability,' but no percentage or rate is given.
The Conclusions state that patients who developed long COVID before October 2021 'continue to be burdened with symptoms,' without quantification.

The Discussion notes that 'the role of access to providers and the economic means to afford long COVID care should continue to be studied' as a contributor to disparate care and outcomes, but the document itself does not supply any such cost or access data.
Caregiver strain, insurance-denial experiences, and long-term financial consequences for patients are not mentioned at all in this document.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, direct non-medical cost (e.g., travel, paid help), or indirect cost (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time) data are reported anywhere in this document; a cost model would require linking this or a comparable U09.9 cohort to billing/claims cost data not present here.

No individual-level financial burden, insurance-denial, or employment-outcome data are reported; only area-level (ZCTA) SDoH proxies (poverty rate, unemployment rate, public insurance rate, college-degree rate) are available, which are ecological, not patient-level, measures.

No national or population-wide long COVID prevalence estimate is given; the cohort is limited to U09.9-coded patients at 34 of 76 N3C sites meeting data-quality criteria, during a roughly 8-month index window (Oct 2021-May 2022).
comparison_boundaries: The 9.7% acute-hospitalization proportion observed in this 34-site N3C EHR cohort (Oct 2021-May 2022 index window) must not be pooled with the 25% figure the document cites from a FAIR Health white paper based on claims data; the paper explicitly contrasts the two as coming from different data sources and only notes the discrepancy, it does not adopt or reconcile the FAIR Health figure as its own estimate.

All demographic and area-level SDoH comparisons (sex, race, ethnicity, poverty, unemployment, insurance, education percentages) are relative to 'all SARS-CoV-2 positive patients at the same 34 N3C sites,' not a national or general-population denominator, and must not be read as national demographic or national prevalence estimates.

The U09.9 cohort (n=33,782, base population) reflects only patients coded between October 1, 2021 and May 26, 2022 at 34 of 76 N3C sites meeting specific data-quality criteria; it is not a national count of long COVID cases and cannot be scaled to a national figure without additional assumptions the document does not make.

Diagnosis-cluster, procedure-utilization, and medication findings are reported separately by age stratum (<21, 21-45, 46-65, 66+); these age-specific patterns should not be collapsed into a single age-blind figure, since the document itself finds the clusters and care patterns differ by age group.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The U09.9 cohort skewed female compared with all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites (66.9% vs. 55.6%; p<0.01). Table 1 additionally breaks down the female percentage by age group within the U09.9 cohort: 57.0% (<21 years), 73.0% (21-45 years), 66.7% (46-65 years), and 60.1% (66+ years).

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The entire cohort and all modeled_issues values above are derived from presence of the ICD-10-CM diagnosis code U09.9 in EHR/claims-integrated N3C data. The document itself states the code was not available until nearly 2 years into the pandemic, that many eligible patients 'missed out' on receiving it, that usage mixes billing and clinical contexts that cannot be distinguished, and that patients in socially deprived areas are underrepresented in the coded cohort despite higher COVID-19 rates in those areas - consistent with claims/ICD-10-coded undercounting via both coding-ambiguity and access-to-diagnosis mechanisms.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The 9.7% acute-hospitalization proportion, the 2.3% severe-hospitalization proportion, the 37.2% lacking a COVID index date, and the 22.8% average radiographic imaging utilization are each reported as single cohort-wide (or age-pooled, in the imaging case) percentages with no cross-tabulation by sex, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a regulatory/classification gap in which no dedicated ICD-10-CM code for long COVID existed for nearly two years after patients began reporting the condition, during which ad hoc placeholder coding (B94.8) was used, and even after U09.9's release in October 2021 treatment guidelines 'remain under development' and clinicians reportedly struggle to apply the code correctly ('physicians don't speak coding').
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Background (p.2) states the ICD-10-CM code for long COVID was not available until October 2021, nearly 2 years after patients began describing the condition; Discussion (p.8) states treatment guidelines for long COVID 'remain under development'; Limitations (p.9) cites a CDC Q&A attendee's statement that 'physicians don't speak coding' and notes a likely disconnect between CDC's intended use of the code and its actual clinical/billing application.

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document could help care delivery teams and payers/policy audiences understand how structural factors - a nearly two-year coding delay, inconsistent clinical uptake, and socioeconomic/demographic disparities in who receives a diagnosis code - shape which long COVID patients are visible in administrative/EHR data at all, informing where surveillance and outreach gaps exist. contextual_issues: The paper notes it cannot distinguish clinical (problem-list) diagnosis codes from billing/reimbursement codes, meaning some U09.9 use may reflect administrative rather than clinical care-seeking burden, but this is not quantified.

Receipt of rehabilitation services (physical/occupational therapy) in the 60 days after U09.9 diagnosis is described as 'rising with patient age,' which the authors say 'lends insight into the burden of functional disability,' but no percentage or rate is given.
The Conclusions state that patients who developed long COVID before October 2021 'continue to be burdened with symptoms,' without quantification.

The Discussion notes that 'the role of access to providers and the economic means to afford long COVID care should continue to be studied' as a contributor to disparate care and outcomes, but the document itself does not supply any such cost or access data.
Caregiver strain, insurance-denial experiences, and long-term financial consequences for patients are not mentioned at all in this document.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, direct non-medical cost (e.g., travel, paid help), or indirect cost (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time) data are reported anywhere in this document; a cost model would require linking this or a comparable U09.9 cohort to billing/claims cost data not present here.

No individual-level financial burden, insurance-denial, or employment-outcome data are reported; only area-level (ZCTA) SDoH proxies (poverty rate, unemployment rate, public insurance rate, college-degree rate) are available, which are ecological, not patient-level, measures.

No national or population-wide long COVID prevalence estimate is given; the cohort is limited to U09.9-coded patients at 34 of 76 N3C sites meeting data-quality criteria, during a roughly 8-month index window (Oct 2021-May 2022).
comparison_boundaries: The 9.7% acute-hospitalization proportion observed in this 34-site N3C EHR cohort (Oct 2021-May 2022 index window) must not be pooled with the 25% figure the document cites from a FAIR Health white paper based on claims data; the paper explicitly contrasts the two as coming from different data sources and only notes the discrepancy, it does not adopt or reconcile the FAIR Health figure as its own estimate.

All demographic and area-level SDoH comparisons (sex, race, ethnicity, poverty, unemployment, insurance, education percentages) are relative to 'all SARS-CoV-2 positive patients at the same 34 N3C sites,' not a national or general-population denominator, and must not be read as national demographic or national prevalence estimates.

The U09.9 cohort (n=33,782, base population) reflects only patients coded between October 1, 2021 and May 26, 2022 at 34 of 76 N3C sites meeting specific data-quality criteria; it is not a national count of long COVID cases and cannot be scaled to a national figure without additional assumptions the document does not make.

Diagnosis-cluster, procedure-utilization, and medication findings are reported separately by age stratum (<21, 21-45, 46-65, 66+); these age-specific patterns should not be collapsed into a single age-blind figure, since the document itself finds the clusters and care patterns differ by age group.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The U09.9 cohort skewed female compared with all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites (66.9% vs. 55.6%; p<0.01). Table 1 additionally breaks down the female percentage by age group within the U09.9 cohort: 57.0% (<21 years), 73.0% (21-45 years), 66.7% (46-65 years), and 60.1% (66+ years).

spec.title: Long COVID Diagnosis Code (U09.9) Coding Delay and Representation Gaps (N3C Cohort, Oct 2021-May 2022)
spec.boundary: This simulator reproduces coding-uptake, demographic-representation, and clinical-encounter figures from a single N3C electronic-health-record study of the U09.9 long COVID diagnosis code at 34 US health systems (index dates Oct 1 2021-May 26 2022, n=33,782 coded patients). It does not include any medical cost, non-medical cost, income-loss, or caregiving-time data, because this document reports none. All demographic comparisons are against the SARS-CoV-2-positive population at the same 34 sites, not a national benchmark, and the cohort cannot be scaled to a national count without assumptions the document does not make.

takeaway.patient: This study looked only at who ended up with an official 'long COVID' diagnosis code in medical records at 34 US health systems, not at cost or at how long any individual patient's path to diagnosis took. It found that patients who received this diagnosis code were disproportionately women and White, and that the code itself did not exist until nearly two years after many patients first reported symptoms. The study does not measure cost, income loss, or caregiving time at all, and it cannot say exactly why these representation patterns exist.
takeaway.care: In this EHR cohort, use of the U09.9 code skewed toward female and White patients at lower-poverty-area sites, relative to the overall SARS-CoV-2-positive population at the same 34 sites. Over a third of coded patients had no documented acute-infection date anywhere in structured data, and imaging/ECG/rehabilitation-utilization patterns varied by age group. The study cannot separate how much of this reflects who returns for the primary-care visits that generate the code versus inconsistent coding practice.
takeaway.policy: Because the dedicated ICD-10-CM long COVID code did not exist for roughly two years after patients began reporting symptoms, and because coded patients in this 34-site EHR cohort skewed female, White, and lower-poverty-area relative to the broader SARS-CoV-2-positive population at the same sites, administrative counts based on this single code likely undercount and skew the true long COVID patient population. The study cannot separate how much of this skew reflects differential care-seeking, access to the primary-care visits that generate the code, or inconsistent coding practice across sites.

patient: If you have ongoing post-COVID symptoms, it may be worth raising with your doctor whether your long COVID symptoms are reflected in your medical record at all, since this study found many affected patients were not formally coded.

If you are male, non-White, or live in a lower-income area, this study's finding that such patients are statistically less represented in diagnosis counts may be useful context if you feel your symptoms have been dismissed or overlooked - the gap reflects measurement patterns, not how real your condition is.

Consider sharing this finding with a long COVID patient advocacy group, since it speaks to who is and is not being counted in official data, which can affect what research and resources get prioritized.
care: This demographic skew finding may be worth checking against your own site's U09.9 coding patterns, to see whether similar gaps by sex, race, or area-level poverty appear in your own patient population.

Given that over a third of coded patients in this study lacked a documented acute-infection date, consider whether your intake workflow reliably links a long COVID diagnosis to earlier infection documentation, to support continuity of care.

Age-stratified differences in imaging, ECG, and rehabilitation-referral patterns reported in this study may be useful as an external benchmark when reviewing your own long COVID care pathway, though they should not be treated as a clinical guideline.
policy: These representation gaps suggest surveillance or program-sizing decisions relying solely on U09.9 counts should treat them as a lower bound, not a complete population count.

Consider funding research that links U09.9-based EHR cohorts to claims or survey data (the document itself cites, but does not reconcile with, a different claims-based hospitalization figure) to better characterize the gap between coded and true long COVID burden.

The reported skew toward lower-poverty-area patients receiving the code may be worth considering when designing outreach or equity-focused long COVID screening programs, alongside the study's own caution that it cannot isolate access, bias, or coding-practice causes individually.

inputs.interpretation: This lets you explore how large a share of the coded cohort lacked any recorded acute-infection date; a higher share strengthens the document's point that EHR-based coding captures an incomplete picture of patients' COVID history.

inputs.label: Share of U09.9 cohort hospitalized during acute infection
inputs.source: Document reports 9.7% (3266/33,782) of the U09.9 cohort were hospitalized during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection (Results, p.4); default from source, 0-30 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's own EHR-based hospitalization share; moving it explores this single-source figure, which the document separately notes should not be pooled with a different claims-based figure it cites but does not adopt.

outputs.label: U09.9 cohort % female minus all-SARS-CoV-2-positive % female (positive = women overrepresented among those coded; negative = underrepresented)
outputs.interpretation: This is the percentage-point gap between the share of female patients coded with U09.9 and the share of female patients among all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites. The document reports an 11.3-point positive gap, meaning women were overrepresented among patients who received the diagnosis code; the document does not isolate why (care-seeking, symptom reporting, or coding practice) and does not claim this measures true sex differences in long COVID prevalence.

outputs.label: U09.9 cohort % White minus all-SARS-CoV-2-positive % White (positive = White patients overrepresented among those coded; negative = underrepresented)
outputs.interpretation: This is the percentage-point gap between the share of White patients coded with U09.9 and the share of White patients among all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites. The document reports a 10.7-point positive gap, meaning White patients were overrepresented among those coded; the document does not isolate why and does not claim this measures true racial differences in long COVID prevalence.

outputs.label: Share of U09.9 patients with no recorded acute-infection date
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of U09.9-coded patients who had no recorded acute SARS-CoV-2 infection date anywhere in their structured EHR data, despite receiving a post-COVID diagnosis code. A higher value means more of the coded population's prior infection history was not captured in structured data, which the authors give as one reason the EHR-coded cohort likely does not represent the true long COVID population.

outputs.label: Share of U09.9 cohort hospitalized during acute infection
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of the U09.9-coded cohort who had been hospitalized during their acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, per this EHR-based cohort only. The document separately cites a different hospitalization percentage from claims data elsewhere, explicitly noting the two figures come from different data sources and should not be pooled together.

outputs.label: Years between symptom reports and dedicated diagnosis code becoming available
outputs.interpretation: This is the approximate number of years between when patients began describing persistent post-COVID symptoms and when a dedicated ICD-10-CM code (U09.9) became available. A longer delay means more patients had no formal code available for their condition during that period, a structural reason the document gives for the coded population undercounting the true long COVID patient population.

scenarios.label: Sex gap, patients under 21
scenarios.goal: Checks whether female overrepresentation among coded patients also appears in the youngest group.
scenarios.description: Table 1 reports 57.0% female among U09.9-coded patients under 21, well below the overall cohort's 66.9%, against the same 55.6% all-COVID female benchmark.

scenarios.label: Sex gap, ages 21-45
scenarios.goal: Shows which age stratum has the largest reported female overrepresentation among coded patients.
scenarios.description: Table 1 reports 73.0% female among U09.9-coded patients aged 21-45, the highest of any age stratum, against the same 55.6% all-COVID female benchmark.

scenarios.label: Severe (ICU-level) hospitalization share
scenarios.goal: Compares overall acute hospitalization with just the most severely ill subset of the same cohort.
scenarios.description: The paper reports 2.3% of all U09.9 patients needed ventilator, ECMO, or vasopressor support, versus 9.7% hospitalized overall, illustrating how much of the hospitalized group was severely ill.

scenarios.label: Illustrative longer coding delay
scenarios.goal: Tests sensitivity of the reported diagnosis-code timeline to an assumed longer delay bound.
scenarios.description: Sets the delay to 2.5 years, an illustrative upper exploration bound rather than a figure the document reports, compared with the document's approximate 2-year estimate.

scenarios.label: Illustrative shorter coding delay
scenarios.goal: Tests sensitivity of the reported diagnosis-code timeline to an assumed shorter delay bound.
scenarios.description: Sets the delay to 1.5 years, an illustrative lower exploration bound rather than a figure the document reports, compared with the document's approximate 2-year estimate.

package.documentation:
## Data source
This simulator is built from a single peer-reviewed retrospective cohort study using the National COVID Cohort Collaborative (N3C) database, covering 33,782 patients coded with ICD-10-CM U09.9 ('Post COVID-19 condition, unspecified') at 34 of 76 N3C-participating US health systems meeting data-quality criteria, with index dates between October 1, 2021 and May 26, 2022.

## What the inputs represent
- Coding delay (years): the document's approximate ~2-year gap between Spring 2020 patient symptom reports and the October 2021 release of the U09.9 code (Background, p.1-2).
- Sex and race shares (U09.9 cohort vs. all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites): Results, p.5.
- Share of U09.9 patients with no recorded acute-infection index date in structured EHR data: Results, p.4-5.
- Share of U09.9 patients hospitalized during acute infection: Results, p.4.
All percentage-input ranges beyond the reported default are assumed exploration bounds chosen for this simulator, not values specified in the document.

## What the outputs represent
The sex and race representation-gap outputs compute the percentage-point difference between the coded cohort's share and the all-SARS-CoV-2-positive comparison share at the same sites; a positive value means overrepresentation in the coded cohort. The missing-index-date, hospitalization, and coding-delay outputs are direct pass-throughs of the document's own reported figures.

## Limitations
This figure is based entirely on presence of the U09.9 ICD-10-CM code in EHR/claims-integrated data. The document itself notes the code was unavailable for nearly two years, that coding mixes clinical and billing use it cannot distinguish, and that patients in socially deprived areas are underrepresented despite higher COVID-19 rates there - all consistent with this coded figure undercounting the true long COVID patient population.

The hospitalization, missing-index-date, and imaging-utilization percentages are each reported as single pooled values with no breakdown by sex, race/ethnicity, disability, or other subgroup; federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports such disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it here.

Separately, the document describes a systemic gap: no dedicated diagnosis code existed for long COVID for nearly two years after patients began reporting it, ad hoc codes were used in the interim, treatment guidelines remain under development, and clinicians reportedly struggle to apply the code consistently ('physicians don't speak coding').

This document reports no direct medical cost, non-medical cost, income-loss, or caregiving-time data; no cost figures appear anywhere in this simulator.

Consider funding research that links U09.9-based EHR cohorts to claims or survey data (the document itself cites, but does not reconcile with, a different claims-based hospitalization figure) to better characterize the gap between coded and true long COVID burden.

The reported skew toward lower-poverty-area patients receiving the code may be worth considering when designing outreach or equity-focused long COVID screening programs, alongside the study's own caution that it cannot isolate access, bias, or coding-practice causes individually.
